questions.stem: Which of the following words can be formed using only the letters present in the word 'CANTEEN'?

options.option_text: NEATLY — an adverb meaning done in a tidy or orderly manner
NEATEN — a verb meaning to make something neat and tidy
TENANT — a person who occupies a rented house or property
ENTICE — a verb meaning to attract or tempt someone cleverly

questions.explanation: B is correct. CANTEEN = C, A, N(×2), T, E(×2). NEATEN needs N×2, E×2, A, T — every one present and within supply. Letter-by-letter check: N✓, E✓, A✓, T✓, E✓, N✓. NEATLY needs L and Y, neither in CANTEEN. TENANT needs T×2 but CANTEEN has only one T — the most tempting wrong choice. ENTICE needs I which is absent entirely.

questions.stem: Three of the following words are valid anagrams of 'SILENT'. Which one is NOT an anagram of SILENT?

options.option_text: LISTEN — meaning to pay attention; a valid rearrangement of SILENT
ENLIST — meaning to join a cause; uses all letters E,N,L,I,S,T
TINSEL — metallic festive decoration; a valid anagram of SILENT
INSECT — a six-legged arthropod; contains C not found in SILENT

questions.explanation: D is correct. SILENT = {S,I,L,E,N,T}. LISTEN = {L,I,S,T,E,N} ✓ valid anagram. ENLIST = {E,N,L,I,S,T} ✓ valid anagram. TINSEL = {T,I,N,S,E,L} ✓ valid anagram. INSECT = {I,N,S,E,C,T} — contains the letter C, which does not exist in SILENT. The trap: INSECT also has 6 letters and shares 5 of them with SILENT, so candidates who do not verify every letter will be fooled.

questions.stem: Three of the four words below are anagrams of each other. Which word does NOT belong to this anagram group?

options.option_text: EARTH — the planet or the soil layer beneath our feet
HEART — the vital organ that pumps blood around the body
HATER — a person who expresses strong dislike or animosity
HASTE — the quality of acting with excessive speed or hurry

questions.explanation: D is correct. EARTH = {A,E,H,R,T}. HEART = {H,E,A,R,T} ✓ same bag. HATER = {H,A,T,E,R} ✓ same bag. All three share the exact letter set {A,E,H,R,T}. HASTE = {H,A,S,T,E} — it contains S where the group has R, making it the odd one out. Classic distractor: HATER looks visually different from EARTH yet IS a genuine anagram; HASTE looks closer (shares H,A,T,E) but the crucial R is replaced by S.

questions.stem: The six letters P, R, E, S, E, T can be rearranged to form one meaningful English word. Which of the following is that word?

options.option_text: TEMPER — to moderate or soften; requires M, which is not present
PRESET — configured in advance before operation; exact letter match
PRESTO — a magic exclamation; requires O, not among the six letters
REPAST — a meal or light feast; requires A, which is not present

questions.explanation: B is correct. Available pool: P×1, R×1, E×2, S×1, T×1. PRESET = P,R,E,S,E,T — each letter used exactly once as supplied ✓. TEMPER needs M (absent). PRESTO is the most tempting wrong answer — it is an anagram of POSTER/REPOST and shares 5 of 6 letters, but it needs O which is absent here. REPAST needs A (absent). Key fingerprint: the given set has exactly two E's; only PRESET uses E twice among all options.

questions.stem: Which of the following options is a valid anagram of the word 'GROAN'?

options.option_text: RANGE — a scale or span of values; requires E but GROAN has no E
ORGAN — a body part or musical keyboard instrument; exact anagram
GROPE — to feel around in darkness; requires P and E, both absent
ANGER — a strong negative emotion; requires E, which GROAN lacks

questions.explanation: B is correct. GROAN = {G,R,O,A,N}. ORGAN = {O,R,G,A,N} — identical five-letter set ✓. Mapping: O✓, R✓, G✓, A✓, N✓. RANGE contains E (absent in GROAN). GROPE contains P and E (both absent). ANGER contains E (absent) and shares A,N,G,R with GROAN — making it the most tempting distractor since it matches 4 of 5 letters. GROAN–ORGAN is a classic anagram pair frequently tested in reasoning sections.

questions.stem: From the letters of the word 'DEMONSTRATE', which of the following words CANNOT be formed?

options.option_text: RESONATED — echoed or reverberated deeply; all nine letters are available
TORMENTED — greatly distressed or pained; uses T×2 and E×2, both allowed
MODERATES — reduces intensity or severity; every letter stays within supply
MENSTRUATE — a biological cycle; requires the letter U, absent from source

questions.explanation: D is correct. DEMONSTRATE = D, E(×2), M, O, N, S, T(×2), R, A — note: no U anywhere. RESONATED uses R,E×2,S,O,N,A,T,D — all within supply ✓. TORMENTED uses T×2, O, R, M, E×2, N, D — looks suspicious with two T's and two E's but both are available ✓ (the primary distractor). MODERATES uses M,O,D,E×2,R,A,T,S ✓. MENSTRUATE = M,E,N,S,T,R,U,A,T,E — demands U, which does not appear even once in DEMONSTRATE. The hardness: candidates who fixate on letter repetition worry about TORMENTED but miss the single absent letter U in the 10-letter MENSTRUATE.

questions.stem: The word 'CARTHORSE' is a well-known perfect anagram of which of the following words?

options.option_text: ORCHESTRA — a large ensemble of musicians; shares identical set of nine letters
HORSEBACK — the riding surface of a horse; contains B and K, both absent
EARTHWORM — a soil-dwelling segmented worm; contains W and M, both absent
PARCHMENT — writing material from animal skin; contains P, M, N, all absent

questions.explanation: A is correct. CARTHORSE = C, A, R(×2), T, H, O, S, E — 9 letters with R appearing twice. ORCHESTRA = O, R(×2), C, H, E, S, T, A — identical letter multiset ✓. This is one of the most celebrated anagram pairs in English. HORSEBACK contains B and K (both absent from CARTHORSE). EARTHWORM contains W and M (both absent). PARCHMENT contains P, M, N (all absent). Critical insight: R appears TWICE in CARTHORSE; a valid answer must also use R twice — ORCHESTRA is the only option that satisfies this and every other letter count. Candidates are tricked by HORSEBACK because it shares a visual substring with CARTHORSE.

questions.stem: Which of the following words can be formed using ONLY the letters present in the word 'SPRING' (each letter used at most once)?

options.option_text: PRISM — contains the letter M, which is absent in SPRING
STING — contains the letter T, which is absent in SPRING
GRINS — uses only G, R, I, N, S which are all present in SPRING
RINKS — contains the letter K, which is absent in SPRING

questions.explanation: C is correct. GRINS uses G, R, I, N, S — all five are present in SPRING (S, P, R, I, N, G). PRISM needs M (not in SPRING). STING needs T (not in SPRING). RINKS needs K (not in SPRING). The most tempting wrong answer is STING since it shares S, I, N, G with SPRING but requires a T that is absent. Quick rule: list the source word's letters, then tick off each letter needed by the candidate word — one failed tick eliminates that option immediately.

questions.stem: If the letters of the word 'PETAL' are rearranged, which of the following meaningful English words is formed?

options.option_text: PLATE — uses all five letters P, L, A, T, E that appear in PETAL
PLANE — requires the letter N, which is not present in PETAL
PLAIT — requires the letter I, which is not present in PETAL
PLUME — requires both U and M, neither of which appears in PETAL

questions.explanation: A is correct. PETAL contains P, E, T, A, L. Rearranging these five letters gives PLATE (P-L-A-T-E). PLANE needs N (absent), PLAIT needs I (absent), PLUME needs U and M (both absent). Students are drawn to PLANE or PLAIT because the PL_ prefix matches, but the third letter reveals the missing letter. Quick rule: sort the source letters alphabetically — A, E, L, P, T — and verify that every letter of the candidate word appears in this sorted set.

questions.stem: If the first and last letters of the word 'SCREAMS' are removed, the remaining letters read in their original order spell which meaningful English word?

options.option_text: CREAMS — result when only the first letter S is removed, not both
SCREAM — result when only the last letter S is removed, not both
CREAM — result after correctly removing both the first and the last S
CRAMS — a rearrangement of the middle letters, not read in original order

questions.explanation: C is correct. SCREAMS is S-C-R-E-A-M-S (7 letters). Removing only the first S gives CREAMS (6 letters). Removing only the last S gives SCREAM (6 letters). Removing BOTH the first and last letter simultaneously leaves C-R-E-A-M = CREAM (5 letters). The two most tempting distractors are SCREAM and CREAMS — students commonly drop just one end. CRAMS traps those who rearrange instead of reading in order. Quick rule: physically cross out the outermost letter on each side before reading what remains left-to-right.

questions.stem: Which of the following pairs of words are perfect anagrams of each other (they use exactly the same letters in the same count, only arranged differently)?

options.option_text: CHAIR and CHAIN — differ because CHAIR has R while CHAIN has N
STEAK and SKATE — both contain exactly the five letters S, T, E, A, K
BRAND and BRAID — differ because BRAND has N while BRAID has I
FLAME and FLARE — differ because FLAME has M while FLARE has R

questions.explanation: B is correct. STEAK = {S, T, E, A, K} and SKATE = {S, K, A, T, E} — identical five-letter multisets. Sorted alphabetically both yield A-E-K-S-T. For the distractors: CHAIR has R but CHAIN has N (one letter replaced). BRAND has N but BRAID has I. FLAME has M but FLARE has R. Each distractor pair has exactly one swapped letter, making visual checking unreliable. Quick rule: sort both words' letters alphabetically and compare the two sorted strings — genuine anagrams produce character-for-character identical results.

questions.stem: Which of the following words can be formed using only the letters found in 'GEOGRAPHY', with no letter used more times than it appears in that word?

options.option_text: PAGEANT — requires N and T, neither of which appears in GEOGRAPHY
TROPHY — requires the letter T, which is completely absent in GEOGRAPHY
GARISH — requires I and S, neither of which is present in GEOGRAPHY
GORGE — needs G, O, R, G, E and GEOGRAPHY supplies exactly two G's

questions.explanation: D is correct. GEOGRAPHY contains G(×2), E(×1), O(×1), R(×1), A(×1), P(×1), H(×1), Y(×1). GORGE requires G, O, R, G, E — two G's are needed, and GEOGRAPHY provides exactly two. PAGEANT needs N and T (both absent). TROPHY needs T (absent). GARISH needs I and S (both absent). The key trap is the duplicate G: students often reject GORGE, assuming G appears only once. Quick rule: count repeated letters in the source word first, then verify whether any option depends on such repetition before eliminating it.

questions.stem: The letters of the word 'ESTABLISH' are rearranged in strict alphabetical order from left to right. At what position does the letter that was originally at the 5th place in ESTABLISH now appear?

options.option_text: 1st position — only possible if A had been the 5th letter of ESTABLISH
4th position — arises from miscounting H or I as coming before B in the alphabet
2nd position — only letter A precedes B when all nine letters are sorted
3rd position — a common error when E is mistakenly ranked before B in sorting

questions.explanation: C is correct. ESTABLISH: E(1), S(2), T(3), A(4), B(5), L(6), I(7), S(8), H(9). The 5th letter is B. Sorting all nine letters alphabetically: A, B, E, H, I, L, S, S, T. B lands at position 2 since only A precedes it. The most tempting error is position 3 — students occasionally think E comes before B, but in the alphabet sequence A-B-C-D-E, B is rank 2 and E is rank 5, so B < E. Position 4 arises from wrongly placing H or I before B. Quick rule: recall that B is the 2nd letter of the alphabet; within any sorted list, B will occupy position 2 unless another B is also present.

questions.stem: In the word 'BLANKETS', the letters at positions 2, 4, 6, and 8 (counted from the left) are extracted and then rearranged to form a meaningful English word. What is that word?

options.option_text: KNEEL — five letters are needed but only four even-position letters exist
LENS — the letters L, N, E, S from positions 2, 4, 6, 8 rearrange to LENS
SKIN — uses K from position 5, which is an odd position, not an even one
BATS — borrows B and A from odd positions 1 and 3, not from even positions

questions.explanation: B is correct. BLANKETS: B(1), L(2), A(3), N(4), K(5), E(6), T(7), S(8). Even positions 2, 4, 6, 8 yield the letters L, N, E, S respectively. Rearranging L-N-E-S spells LENS. KNEEL is wrong — it has 5 letters but only 4 are extracted. SKIN uses K from position 5 (odd). BATS uses B(1), A(3), T(7) — all from odd positions — plus only S(8) from an even position, so three of its four letters come from the wrong positions. Quick rule: underline every alternate letter starting from position 2 (i.e., the 2nd, 4th, 6th, 8th letters), collect them as a group, and then hunt for a recognizable anagram.
